segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an advocate, a certain Tertullus, and they presented their case against Paul to the governor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Paul had been called in, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Because of you we enjoy great peace, and through your foresight reforms are being made for this nation.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, we welcome this with all gratitude.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But so as not to detain you any longer, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For we have found this man to be a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He even tried to desecrate the temple, and we seized him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about all these things we accuse him of.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jews also joined in the attack, asserting that these things were so.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the governor nodded to him to speak, Paul replied:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I gladly make my defense.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As you are able to find out, it is no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: They did not find me debating with anyone or stirring up a crowd—not in the temple, not in the synagogues, not anywhere in the city.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Nor can they prove to you the things they are now accusing me of.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But this I admit to you: according to the Way, which they call a sect, I serve the God of our ancestors, believing everything that accords with the Law and everything written in the Prophets,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and having a hope in God, which these men themselves also hold, that there is going to be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason I too always strive to keep a clear conscience before God and people.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Now after several years I came to bring gifts for the poor to my nation, and to present offerings.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: While I was occupied with these, they found me in the temple, ritually purified, with no crowd and no uproar.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But there were some Jews from Asia—they are the ones who ought to be here before you to accuse me, if they have anything against me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Or let these men themselves say what crime they found when I stood before the council,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: unless it was this one thing I shouted as I stood among them: ‘It is about the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Felix, who was rather accurately informed about the Way, adjourned the hearing, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody, but to allow him some freedom and not to prevent any of his own people from attending to his needs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as Paul discussed righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go away for now; when I find an opportunity, I will send for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At the same time he was also hoping that Paul would give him money; for that reason he sent for him quite often and talked with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and wanting to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

notes.note: The Greek word means a trained public speaker, and in a courtroom setting it was the ordinary term for a professional who pleaded cases for clients. “Orator” now suggests a maker of fine speeches, not legal counsel, so “advocate” is used; other modern versions have “attorney” or “lawyer”.

The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is usually translated “Gentiles”. In the singular it means a people or nation, and in this chapter (verses 2, 10 and 17) it refers to the Jewish people.

Speeches before a Roman official conventionally opened with compliments designed to win the judge’s goodwill, and “most excellent” was the standard form of address for a governor. Tertullus’s praise is formula, not description: other ancient sources portray Felix’s governorship as harsh and marked by unrest.

The Greek word meant a school of thought or party and is used elsewhere in Acts of the Pharisees and Sadducees without any negative sense. It had not yet acquired the later meaning “heresy”, though Tertullus uses it dismissively and Paul in verse 14 declines the label. “Nazarenes” as a name for the followers of Jesus of Nazareth occurs only here in the New Testament.

Verse 7 is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not included in the Greek text translated here. Later manuscripts add, from the end of verse 6 to the start of verse 8, “and wanted to judge him according to our law. But the tribune Lysias came and with great violence took him out of our hands, ordering his accusers to come before you.” With the longer text, “from him” in verse 8 could refer to Lysias instead of Paul.

“The Way” is the name Acts uses for the movement of Jesus’s followers as they themselves spoke of it (also in verse 22). Paul’s point is that it is not a breakaway party but the right way of serving Israel’s God in keeping with the Scriptures.

Most English versions have “worship” here. The Greek verb means to render religious service to a god, whether by rites or by a whole life of devotion, and it is a different word from the one translated “worship” in verse 11, which names the act of bowing in reverence. “Serve” keeps the two apart.

The traditional “alms” is accurate but has largely dropped out of modern English. The word means charitable gifts to those in need. This is probably a reference to the collection Paul gathered from his largely Gentile churches for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem, which his letters discuss at length but Acts mentions only here.

Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I (the Herod of Acts 12) and sister of the Agrippa and Bernice who appear in chapter 25. According to the Jewish historian Josephus, Felix persuaded her to leave her first husband, the king of Emesa, to marry him. This gives point to Paul’s chosen topics in verse 25.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). Here the word may mean right conduct in general or, since Felix was a judge who hoped for a bribe (verse 26), “justice” in the narrower sense; some translations choose the latter. The same family lies behind “the righteous and the unrighteous” in verse 15.

The two years are most naturally those of Paul’s custody in Caesarea, and this is the usual view. A minority of scholars take the phrase to refer to the length of Felix’s term as governor. The date of Festus’s arrival is itself uncertain, usually placed between AD 55 and 60.

candidates.reason: Used in Acts of the Sadducees, Pharisees and Christians and in the letters of divisive factions; versions vary between “sect”, “party”, “faction” and “heresy”, and the reader should be able to see it is one word.
Recurs through Acts 21–25 and in the Gospels and Revelation; versions split between “tribune”, “commander” and “captain”, and the choice should match the treatment of “centurion”.
Frequent in the Gospels and Acts; a decision is needed between “council” and the loanword “Sanhedrin”, and for local councils (Matthew 10:17).
Traditional “alms” is obsolete for many readers; the word recurs in Matthew 6, Luke and Acts and needs one modern equivalent (“gifts for the poor”, “charitable giving”, “acts of mercy”).

Means the inhabited world and often in practice the Roman Empire (Luke 2:1; Acts 17:6); versions vary between “world”, “inhabited earth” and “empire”, and it should be distinguished consistently from κόσμος.

warnings: Verse 14: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
Verse 6: πειράζω is not rendered with a register form (test; tempt; tempter; put to the test; examine; try / attempt) and has no register-exception note.
